title: Learning from Parker by listening: All God's Children Got Rhythm
summary: At a St. Louis rehearsal Parker takes up a tune Malachi plays and tells him to stop calling changes because his playing came from feeling.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Charlie Parker was quite different. You learned from him by listening to him. He wasn't one to answer a lot of questions, because I don't think Charlie had too much tolerance for ignorance or stupidity, you know. But if you were around him and you listened to him, whether he was talking or playing, if you were quiet and listened, you'd learn a hell of a lot.

One incident happened when we were rehearsing in St. Louis once. Just before the rehearsal, waiting for some of the guys to get there, I was playing the piano, and this tune that I had learned from...I think it was from one of the Marx Brothers movies in which the Duke Ellington band played. It was a tune called "All God's Children Got Rhythm." I had learned this tune back in Washington, because I used to learn every tune I could think so. So I was sitting there playing it, and I liked the chords in it. And Dizzy came over and he said, "Boy, I like that tune." He got his horn, and then he started to playing it. He said, "Call the changes off to me." So I was very happy to do it. I'm sitting and I'm playing, and I say, "This is the F, and D-minor, whatever..." Finally, after a couple of choruses Dizzy had it and he was playing it.

So after Dizzy had played about, oh, seven or eight choruses on it, just he and I sitting at the piano, Charlie Parker came over and said, 'Let's see that. Boy, that's a nice tune. What is it?' And I told him. And he went and got his horn. So Dizzy stopped, and he started playing it, and when he did, I started calling the chord changes. So Charlie said 'Unh-uh. No, don't do that.' I said, 'What?' He said, 'Just play the tune.' So I sat and played the changes. Of course, after a chorus or so, Charlie Parker was just burning it up. But he had that kind of a feeling and an ear, that the chord changes I think didn't matter very much to him. What he played was a reflection of the chord changes, or the harmonic structure of the tune that he heard, you know. A lot of times, what he played might not have anything to do with the chord. It was a feeling, it had just come from a pure feeling.

Well, I had never been exposed to anyone who played like that, because I had been around people who played chord changes. You know, the chord changes were this, then you would hear what was happening, and that was it. But being around Charlie, I learned that Charlie's concept of playing was...his horn was just a metal pipe with keys on it, and whatever he heard, he played! It had nothing to do with any chords or anything.
